body:
As @alexcrichton notes above, the in-tree testing story still has some way to go, so I manually tested that this change works using the following sequence of steps:

1. First, I built the latest HEAD of [`wasi-libc`](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-libc) with threads enabled:

  ```console
  $ git rev-parse HEAD
  05b3b876e63cdc919c79f5127a7ae8dbdb7b095f
  $ make THREAD_MODEL=posix
  ```

2. Then, in this repository, I altered my `config.toml` to use this new sysroot:

  ```console
  // first, enabled building the linker by setting `lld = true` in the [rust] section; then:
  $ echo '[target.wasm32-wasi]' >> config.toml
  $ echo 'wasi-root = "/.../wasi-libc/sysroot"' >> config.toml
  ```

3. Then, I built the Rust toolchain with all of the changes in this PR along with the flags to activate them:

  ```console
  $ RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+atomics,+bulk-memory" ./x.py build library --target wasm32-wasi
  $ rustup toolchain link stage1 build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage1
  ```

5. Using the same [`kernel.rs`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/102157#issue-1383047794) example from #102157, I was able to successfully compile a Rust program that uses shared memory:

  ```console
  $ rustc +stage1 kernel.rs -o kernel.wasm --target wasm32-wasi --crate-type=cdylib  -C link-args="--shared-memory" -C target-feature='+atomics,+atomics'
  $ wasm2wat --enable-threads kernel.wasm | grep '(memory'
    (import "env" "memory" (memory (;0;) 17 16384 shared))
  ```

body:
I think one option would be to make it clear that it's unstable, by having `target_feature = "atomics"` punt us into [restricted-std](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/0ca356586fed56002b10920fd21ddf6fb12de797/library/std/build.rs#L37-L48) mode. This would make `std` be considered [unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/0ca356586fed56002b10920fd21ddf6fb12de797/library/std/src/lib.rs#L192), and require `#![feature(restricted_std)]` to use on wasm+atomics. The benefit of this is that people would understand that it isn't a case of "the target just doesn't ship with a `libstd` so you need to build it" and is really "using std on this target is not stable".

This may be overkill though, or the wrong approach entirely[^1]. Basically, it makes me very uncomfortable to allow this to compile (even with all this) to consider allowing this to build before someone has gone through and audited `std` (and the dependencies of `std` that are used on wasm platforms) for places where we assume that wasm has no threads, and don't bother bother with locks/TLS/something else. (Like, are we really comfortable, even on nightly, letting Rust users use a `std` which just might be wildly thread unsafe?)

I've nominated this for discussion at next week's libs meeting, and will try to do all or part of that audit before then.

[^1]: Like, if we do audit for this, IDK if it would need to be restricted (altho, I guess I don't know why some of the existing restricted targets are...), since I don't think it will be *hard* to determine "is this using a lock" or w/e. (I guess part of it might be that the ecosystem is *full* of code that is thread safe on wasm, since I believe our locks panic there, which pushed people to use `static mut`s and such... That's not *really* `std`s problem, but it is unfortunate)
author: thomcc

body:
> (Like, are we really comfortable, even on nightly, letting Rust users use a std which just might be wildly thread unsafe?)

Well, considering that no one was using this `std`, since it wouldn't compile until this PR, I wasn't too concerned about the possibility of many users seeing issues. I will admit that I'm not too familiar with the restrictions you are talking about, so if you are convinced that things should/could be safer, I'm interested in whatever you suggest (especially if you do the audit, since I'm not exactly clear how "wild" things need to be to be "wildly unsafe").
author: abrown

body:
FWIW I am the original author of threaded support for wasm in the standard library, so vetting all dependencies and making sure everything works was my responsibility and unless anything major has changed in the meantime it should still be the case that for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` things should work. This is a different target, `wasm32-wasi`, and @abrown is the one authoring the support in `wasi-libc` to get threads integrated there.

I would personally consider it overkill to move this to `restricted_std` due to how unusable that form of a target is -- you can't retroactively add `#![feature]` declarations to crates on crates.io. I'm also more than happy to vouch for both the correctness of this patch and helping to shepherd along any threads-related issues in the wasm target. 

I'll also point out that the wasm-with-threads story is in general "not ready" at large. The `threads` proposal itself to WebAssembly has not "officially shipped" and additionally toolchains have not at this time generally figured out how to get traction. The target support in Rust is largely "you know everything about what you're doing and you're trying to get something working" which is a far cry from the stability of `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` for example. Ideally there wouldn't be too much process around fixing/updating things for threads-on-wasm since we're all trying to figure everything out at the same time and it'll never really be certain that everything is "perfect"
author: alexcrichton

body:
> unless anything major has changed in the meantime it should still be the case that for wasm32-unknown-unknown things should work.
> ...
> I'm also more than happy to vouch for both the correctness of this patch and helping to shepherd along any threads-related issues in the wasm target.

Both of these are very good to hear, and pretty much alleviate my concerns.

> The threads proposal itself to WebAssembly has not "officially shipped" and additionally toolchains have not at this time generally figured out how to get traction. The target support in Rust is largely "you know everything about what you're doing and you're trying to get something working"...

So, on the one hand, I had understood that this *is* the kind of situation that restricted_std is for. But I'm sympathetic to the fact that it could cause a ton of ecosystem churn (both now to add the `feature(restricted_std)` under wasm+threads and then later to remove it, when the target becomes ready for broader use), and that there would be no way to experiment around this stuff in the meantime. I think this means that perhaps `restricted_std` isn't really a great way to do things!

Given that it *does* already require nightly to compile (due to needing `-Zbuild-std`), I probably am inclined to agree that this is overkill, but we should be somewhat careful before shipping a build that users can actually use.

I'll leave the nomination for now, but I expect we'll land this. FWIW, If you'd like to attend the meeting, you're more than welcome -- we don't have video meetings for T-libs anymore (only t-libs-api currently has those), so it's just a matter of being on zulip around 8AM PT on Weds in the [t-libs/meetings](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/259402-t-libs.2Fmeetings) zulip stream. (But no worries if you can't -- I think the discussion perhaps should be more about when we should/should not be using `restricted_std`)

author: RalfJung

body:
> Hm, I wish we could at least test that we're seeing roughly expected behavior -- in particular, I worry that we might actually be wrong on big-endian given the sometimes low-level byte manipulation const does, and if we hide a bunch of tests we'd not notice.

FWIW, Miri runs its test suite on the mips64-unknown-linux-gnuabi64 target, and I don't recall a single issue. Endianess is only relevant in very few places in the interpreter -- basically, when loading a multi-byte scalar value from memory, and when storing a multi-byte scalar value to memory. Nothing else works on multiple bytes of memory at a time. https://github.com/rust-lang/miri-test-libstd runs the libcore and liballoc tests on a big-endian target, too (specifically mips-unknown-linux-gnu).  And a bunch of ecosystem crates run their tests on mips64-unknown-linux-gnuabi64 with Miri to test their own big-endianess-compatibility. So I am reasonably confident that the interpreter works correctly for those targets.

Of course it would be nice to have some in-tree tests, but if we include out-of-tree tests we are well-covered currently. Maybe we should run the mips64-unknown-linux-gnuabi64 Miri test suite on rustc CI?

body:
Yeah that is supposed to print the actual memory contents, byte for byte. It would be bad if that didn't match the actual endianess of the interpreted code. This is also entirely untyped.

The only thing we can do here is adjust the tests to make the contents endianess-independent. But that might not always be possible when enum discriminant values are involved. We can also add stderr normalization filters.
author: RalfJung

body:
Uhm, so not sure what the best way to proceed here is. Normalization sounds enticing, but from the output it does not look like there is a trivial way to make it apply generically without significant effort, am I right? The best that could have with the current infrastructure are replacement rules such as these

```
"78 00 00 00 ff ff ff ff" -> "00 00 00 78 ff ff ff ff"
```

which is

1. tedious
2. error prone
3. requires actual big-endian machine to generate these
4. will not apply to any future tests...

Just ignoring these tests solves some of the issues (1, 2, 3), but not the others (4).

body:
> Yeah that is supposed to print the actual memory contents, byte for byte. It would be bad if that didn't match the actual endianess of the interpreted code. This is also entirely untyped.

Maybe I'm just naive, but why do we want this? It seems to me like the root problem is that we're trying to test a portable language using a non-portable output. If we want to test that the behavior of a Rust program is correct, can we print/dump the consts using their Debug impl when possible? Of course this can't necessarily work for all consts, so maybe we should have something like a flag that opts into Debug-dumping consts and we always use in tests?

Trying to hack around the non-portability of dumping the bytes just feels like repeating the old mistake of accidentally writing endian-sensitive code, which we often advertise Miri as a solution to.
author: saethlin

body: The behavior of rustc const eval *is* endianess-dependent -- that is a feature, not a bug. And we want const-eval to sometimes dump the raw low-level bytes of a constant; that's not a bug, either. Of course we also want to test that this output looks the way it should. So I don't quite understand what you mean.

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body: Wouldn't *not parking* the thread if some underlying resource can't be acquired be a valid strategy? After all park is allowed to wake up any time, similar to condvars. So instead of panicing it would return immediately.
author: the8472

body: @the8472 Yes, but if the error keeps occuring, that'd effectively turn a park-loop into a spin-loop, which is pretty bad.

body:
> Wouldn't _not parking_ the thread if some underlying resource can't be acquired be a valid strategy? After all park is allowed to wake up any time, similar to condvars. So instead of panicing it would return immediately.

Yes, definitely, and this is still valid behaviour. However, since implementing that would impact so many different areas (TLS for instance), I doubt that it is really worth it, as errors should be extremely rare here.
author: joboet

body:
> > Wouldn't _not parking_ the thread if some underlying resource can't be acquired be a valid strategy? After all park is allowed to wake up any time, similar to condvars. So instead of panicing it would return immediately.
> 
> Yes, definitely, and this is still valid behaviour. However, since implementing that would impact so many different areas (TLS for instance), I doubt that it is really worth it, as errors should be extremely rare here.

What about eagerly allocating the resources when creating the thread?

body:
> What about eagerly allocating the resources when creating the thread?

That doesn't prevent all possible panics. We can't guarantee that e.g. the underlying libc calls always succeed. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/102398#issuecomment-1271642165

body:
Don't run your local rustfmt manually, it won't be the correct version and you'll miss parameters (e.g. the edition), causing the errors above.

Use `./x.py fmt` instead. There's more info in the [dev guide here](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/intro.html?highlight=rustfmt#formatting).

body:
I spent some time looking into this today. Things to note:

- `-Ztime-passes -Zno-interleave-lints` is a good combination. It prints out the expensive lints.

- The `UnusedBrokenConst` lint is the main culprit here. If you disable just that you still get something like 60% of the wins. I don't understand how this lint works, though clearly it's triggering lots of CTFE. If I disable it I get lots of `ui` test failures, but this is only because the `ui` tests use `--emit metadata`. If I just do a normal compilation of the failing `ui` test source files I get the same output as normal.

- This PR understates the cost of lints. It comments out all the `check_*` functions, but each lint still does a no-check traversal of the AST/HIR, which has a non-trivial cost. I tried a variant that instead stops all the lint traversals from happening, and the savings were about 1.25x better than in this PR.

The obvious follow-up questions.

- Can `UnusedBrokenConst` be made cheaper? It seems incredibly expensive for what it's doing.

- Can the general AST/HIR traversal cost be reduced? It seems suboptimal to have dozens of lints, each of which fully traverses the AST/HIR but only checks a fraction of the AST/HIR nodes. Can we invert the iteration, i.e. traverse the AST/HIR once, and only iterate over the relevant lints for each node?
author: nnethercote

body:
`UnusedBrokenConst` is a red herring. What that 'lint' does is go over all consts in the crate and trigger their evaluation. This is needed, we must report errors in constants no matter whether they are used or not:
- for `cargo check`, this might be the only way constants are evaluated at all -- if we skip this step, we are just not emitting diagnostics that will then show up later during `cargo build` (when the same constants are evaluated because codegen needs them). Of course skipping this step makes rustc a lot faster, but if that is the kind of optimization we are looking for then I propose we also skip borrow-checking all the code, that will also give us some nice perf wins. ;)
- for `cargo build`, this only affects constants that are unused (hence the name), but also for those we stably promise that they are evaluated and will lead to a deny-by-default error (hard error once https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/102091 lands), which is crucial for 'static assertions'.

body:
I think in general probably every case where we do something different depending on GITHUB_ACTIONS being set isn't right (unless its for things like turning off color or so); we should rely on a src/ci/run.sh-set variable for that (or config.toml option).

So I'm in general in favor of the direction of this PR, but I would prefer that we go farther and entirely decouple from github actions-only environment variables in rustbuild itself (and if not possible, discuss that on a case by case basis).
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body: @Mark-Simulacrum if I understand what you're saying, is that you would rather require that an environment variable like RUST_LANG_CI be defined explicitly to enable specific "official" CI checks separately from detecting and enabling those checks by default in a CI environment based on environment variables like GITHUB_ACTIONS? Let me know what modifications you would like to have made, and I'll modify my pull request
author: awakecoding

body: Of course, if you have a fairly good idea of how you would like to address this specific issue and would rather open a separate pull request with the changes, that is fine with me as well. It doesn't need to be fixed by this specific pull request, all I care about is not having to undefine GITHUB_ACTIONS to avoid triggering the official rust-lang CI checks, it's hackish and makes custom CI builds harder
author: awakecoding

body: Yes, that sounds right. I don't have a lot of bandwidth to hunt down each case we rely on the GitHub actions set environment variables to make the determination - I think hopefully it's not too hard for you to make a reasonable decision in most of those places and switch them to using something like RUST_LANG_CI. We can iterate from there.

I've not had a chance to look at this in detail, but want to voice some concerns based on a cursory glance.

The Rust Style Guide has some [very explicit prescription for match expressions](https://github.com/rust-dev-tools/fmt-rfcs/blob/master/guide/expressions.md#match), including the various scenarios on when to use braces.

body:
> I don't know if macro arguments need to abide by the style guide

Understand the technical distinction you are drawing. However, I'm trying to look at this from the perspective of developer expectations. Despite being an arg, I think it's also fair to say that most devs will still look at that arg as a stereotypical match expression, would manually format it as they would any other match expression outside a call arg context, and would expect automated tooling to format it as such as well.

rustfmt would by default format such an arg according to the match expr rules if a different delimiter were used for the call (rustfmt leaves calls using brace delims alone as part of an escape hatch). If they'd written `match_ast!(....)` instead of `match_ast!{...}` then we'd have a conflict between the lint and tooling defaults just within the relatively small diff of this PR, so I do worry about the broader churn this could potentially introduce.

More generally, would the proposed changes not impact the same type of match expr outside a call arg context?

Usually LLVM manages to figure out inlining for tiny functions like this on its own; `#[inline]` and `#[inline(always)]` hints are useful when it *doesn't* figure things out.

I'd recommend trying some experiments with godbolt, typing code at rustc and seeing what the assembly looks like, and if you see a call to a tiny stub function that *should* be inlined but isn't, that's a good place to add `#[inline]`.

body: I guess my question should have been phrased as "Why was that function not inlined in the first place (without an inline attribute), since this is also generic?". Apologies for the poor formulation. Is there a difference between blanket impls and generic impls (i.e. `impl Foo for T` vs `impl Foo for Option<T>`)?
author: bugadani

body: No, there is no difference between those. LLVMs inliner (and MIR inlining) just inline whatever their heuristics say should be inlined, which is often correct, but not always. Functions being generic just _allows_ inlining in the first place (because the function implementation has to by copied into the user codegen unit), whether it actually happens is up to the inliner.
author: Noratrieb

body:
> @SoniEx2 I'd be _mildly_ surprised that this isn't already being inlined. Do you have some code in release mode where this isn't being inlined?

A lot of our generic methods don't end up getting inlined when optimizing for size. At a previous job I was doing a lot of embedded stuff, and at -Copt-level=z (even with -Zbuild-std) we'd frequently see dozens of copies of tiny generic functions. FWIW, this would only happen on certain targets (I guess the set of LLVM passes we run depends somewhat on the target? Since not all targets exhibited this issue), which makes the issue more annoying.

Some (but not all) of these would be inlined anyway, but end up in the output regardless, but this is an LLVM bug (some discussion in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/96624). This was never that big of a deal (cost was likely under a kilobyte of code total which didn't make a difference for us), so I never dug that deeply (also IMO ideally we wouldn't need to mark these with `#[inline]`, and hopefully won't in the future).

While I never saw Option::from, I suspect this is just because it doesn't get used much in that code, since this is absolutely the kind of thing we'd see copies of.
author: thomcc

body:
Because this is a recurring problem, I've spent some time trying to understand just why `#[inline]` makes a difference for generic functions, even though it ostensibly shouldn't. This is my conclusion: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/102539

Basically, if we ignore the opt-for-size case (where `-Z share-generics` causes extra issues), the relevant distinction is whether the function is instantiated per-crate or per-CGU. Generic functions are instantiated per-crate, while `#[inline]` functions are instantiated per-CGU.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body:
> In Ferrocene some of the documentation can contain `file://` links when built locally

Can this be set up so that it only applies to Ferrocene docs? I don't want `file://` URLs to accidentally leak into rustdoc, which is supposed to generate relocatable docs.
author: notriddle

body:
If `file://` links are not wanted in rustdoc then we can probably just close this PR :slightly_smiling_face:

To be clear, we already made this change in the Ferrocene repository, so our use case is already covered! As a policy we'd like to keep as little changes as possible proprietary, so we try to upstream the patches we make. Of course it's then up to the relevant team to decide whether the patch makes sense upstream, like in this case. I mentioned Ferrocene needs it to provide context on why I'm proposing this change, rather than saying we actively need this PR to be merged.
author: emilyalbini

body:
I'm also a bit reluctant to accidentally allow `file:` urls from sneaking in, but I also agree that is unlikely.

I'm not sure what you are doing that would result in `file:` urls from appearing in your documentation. Usually those are pretty terrible things to have, as they are usually absolute, and not compatible with localhost serving. Ideally I would recommend looking at trying to avoid them if at all possible.

Can you at least add a comment explaining why they are being ignored? The other schemes make sense, but seeing `file:` there sticks out as unlike the others and not something I would expect (or want) in our documentation to ever appear.
author: ehuss

body:
> I'm not sure what you are doing that would result in file: urls from appearing in your documentation. Usually those are pretty terrible things to have, as they are usually absolute, and not compatible with localhost serving. Ideally I would recommend looking at trying to avoid them if at all possible.
>
> Can you at least add a comment explaining why they are being ignored? The other schemes make sense, but seeing file: there sticks out as unlike the others and not something I would expect (or want) in our documentation to ever appear.

One of the pieces of documentation we need to produce for Ferrocene is a report linking test files with the relevant sections of the Ferrocene spec. When the report is produced by CI those links point to the source code on GitHub, but when building the report locally we use `file://` links. That way, when clicking on the file you open it directly with your local editor.

I totally get wanting to avoid those links showing up in Rust's documentation, so if you prefer I can close the PR and keep this patch only in our repository.
author: emilyalbini

body:
Do those links point to somewhere outside (your version of) the Rust checkout?

If they're pointing to files in the checkout that upstream Rust just doesn't have, I wonder if we could make linkchecker smarter and handle that case.

If they're pointing to files *outside* the checkout, I do think we shouldn't allow that here, since any instance of it upstream would be a bug.

Using josh only for one direction will not work well I think.

body:
This looks like a bug in the stable hasher.  This branch is only used for item-relative spans (`-Zincremental-relative-spans`).  Using a `unwrap_or(DUMMY_SP)` is safe: span hashing won't try to make this a relative span.
The better solution would ofc to find a way to modify `resolutions(()).source_span`.

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features

Another reason might be that BOLT is more effective for binaries than for shared libraries. I'll try to statically link rustc and apply BOLT to it, to see what happens.

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body: Various versions of the `tendril` crate are causing 380 of the 470 regressions (they actually do use unaligned references). The rest are various smaller (<=5 dependents) crates or just spurious build.rs/proc macro failures
author: oli-obk

body:
Looks like this got fixed in tendril 0.4.3 half a year ago by [removing the use of `packed`](https://github.com/servo/tendril/commit/bdd07bfcc8b9bd43961248e92a82ed2b936e1868). So at least for the users of the 0.4 series, there is a semver-compatible fix available. According to download stats 0.4.3 is the only version downloaded in relevant quantities, though the crater run shows that a bunch of stale lockfiles still contain 0.4.1 and older versions.

So this is another case of, crater also tests unmaintained parts of the ecosystem with a lockfile, and there is basically nothing we can do to get those parts to update.
author: RalfJung

body:
Here are the tendril version stats from the regressed crates
```
      1 Checking tendril v0.1.6
      7 Checking tendril v0.2.4
     46 Checking tendril v0.3.1
     15 Checking tendril v0.4.0
    294 Checking tendril v0.4.1
```
So a bit more than 50 don't have a semver-compatible update. These are almost all on github; in terms of crates.io there are only 6:
```
reg/snoot/0.1.2/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
reg/webgl_generator/0.2.0/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
reg/femto-feed/0.3.0/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
reg/rbatis_xml_parser/0.1.0/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
reg/aocl/0.1.1/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
reg/html2runes/1.0.1/try#c34df645207dd0b6887b2312cf109109ba3a0ffb.txt
```
These all have fairly few recent downloads, and except for rbatis_xml_parser they have not been updated in years. rbatis_xml_parser points to a non-existent github repo so I guess we can also consider it dead.
author: RalfJung

body:
@rust-lang/lang I'd like to get approval for making the 'unaligned_references' lint a hard error. It has been warn-by-default since Rust 1.53 (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/82525) and deny-by-default with mention in cargo future-incompat reports since Rust 1.62 (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/95372). Current nightly will become Rust 1.66. This finally closes one of our oldest soundness gaps, an oversight that goes back all the way to Rust 1.0.

See above for a detailed analysis of the crater results, the summary is that the majority of the regressions (380 of 470) is caused by a single crate, `tendril`.  Its latest version 0.4.3 (released half a year ago) is fixed, and 85% of the `tendril` regressions would be fixed by a simple `cargo update`. The remaining crate regressions are rarely used and/or unmaintained crates.

body:
The dependency is going through various indirections... unfortunately `cargo tree` does not seem to work for target-specific dependencies, so I don't have the full picture, but one chain is "hyper 0.12 -> tokio 0.1 -> mio 0.6 -> winapi 0.2". Hyper 0.12 still has [3k downloads on weekdays](https://crates.io/crates/hyper/0.12.36) so breaking it is probably not an option...

Not sure if a mio 0.6 patch release that bumps winapi is realistic. Honestly a winapi 0.2 patch release is probably the least amount of work and seems prudent given how fundamental that crate is for the windows ecosystem (which crater does not probe).

body:
I'm not an expert in our `derive` infrastructure, so -- not sure. It could also lead to surprises when someone writes something like
```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
#[repr(packed)]
struct MyStr(String);
```
and there is no error but the generated `Debug` implementation is just not usable. Though maybe taht can somehow be resolved? After all this also prints a nice error
```rust
struct MyType;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct SndType(MyType);
```

Being more clever wrt. packed in our derive macros would also help with [this problem](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/82523#issuecomment-1311419639).

body:
Its actually crazy because I half-fixed this completely independently locally, when working on something else.

I don't think we should stop printing placeholders as bound vars. They're sort of an "internal detail" of how we solve higher-ranked bounds. What instead would you want to show the user? The lifetime name must come from somewhere.
author: jackh726

body:
> I don't think we should stop printing placeholders as bound vars. They're sort of an "internal detail" of how we solve higher-ranked bounds. What instead would you want to show the user? The lifetime name must come from somewhere.

Haven't thought too deeply about this, but: Ideally we only show placeholders to users after already introducing the binder somewhere. E.g. if they are part of the trace of a selection error, we should start with the higher ranked obligation which uses `for<'a>` and then can just use `'a` without adding a new binder for nested obligations. So we should print placeholders without mentioning their binder at all. Though the infcx should remember all placeholders it created so that we can deal with duplicate names

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body:
Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

> This is reasonable for how we've been doing inlines in libs, and there's nothing scary to me about those instruction results (clearly more good than bad), so
> 
> r? @scottmcm @bors r+ rollup=never

Hey, @scottmcm : it looks to me like the final results were ... still more good than bad, but not quite *as* good as what was predicted from the earlier run. Namely, the earlier run reported 37 primary improvements, but the end PR only says 14 primary improvements.

Overall, I think it looks like something we still go ahead with. In some ways the biggest decision is whether to be concerned about that 1.8% hit to the build-time for `serde_derive`, which is a cost you were already saying you were willing to bear before; I just want to make sure you're still willing to bear it for a somewhat lesser win.

I'm curious how, for serde_derive, opt-full was +1.76% but opt-**incr**-full was -0.05% (below significance threshold).

I do still think this makes sense, based on the analysis from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/102539#issuecomment-1264398807 that inspired this PR in the first place.  But it's always hard for me to judge these, so I'm mostly just leaning on "well, it said -0.1% overall" and that the diff is perfectly reasonable, so could plausibly be persuaded otherwise if anyone feels strongly.

body:
Okay, syncing onto an already existing sync branch is not a thing -- josh will complain
```
remote: hint: Updates were rejected because a pushed branch tip is behind its remote
remote: hint: counterpart. Check out this branch and integrate the remote changes
remote: hint: (e.g. 'git pull ...') before pushing again.
remote: hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.
```
I don't quite understand why this is a problem, given that even when it succeeds the pushed tip does not contain a sync from the rustc repo, but :shrug: . We want to always use the 'remote counterpart does not exist yet, use `-o base`' mode, I think.

I did update my master branch to the latest one first so it could have picked a newer one. There seems to be nothing wrong with using that particular commit, but I'd like to understand why it didn't use the latest one...

@tmandry I am still very confused how `llvm_has_rust_patches` is meant to be used. The only place I see it used is in `Build::is_rust_llvm`, which is used in three places:
1. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/c5f92ce2a075c0f656362513ebbaf19006eab047/src/bootstrap/test.rs#L1553-L1554
2. The new assert I just added. Let's ignore that for now.
3. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/b3bc6bf31265ac10946a0832092dbcedf9b26805/src/bootstrap/compile.rs#L805-L806

3 defines LLVM_RUSTLLVM, which is eventually used in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/693c6311f06bf49ff0fd7b972d769634e4b330b1/compiler/rustc_llvm/llvm-wrapper/PassWrapper.cpp#L308-L311; that bit looks correct. But 1. looks absolutely wrong even before this PR: it will pass `--system-llvm` for an in-tree commit with `submodules = false` and `patches = false`. How is `llvm_has_rust_patches` tested? how is it supposed to work? I ran `llvm-config --ldflags --system-llvm` locally and it didn't even exit successfully ...

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body:
@bors r+ rollup=never

Seems OK. I do wonder if we should be adding a safe-transmute like intrinsic that core uses here, rather than producing impls for an ever-increasing number of types (and only ones in the standard library, so user-defined enums don't get the same benefit). It seems pretty easy for the compiler to say "yep" and likely much lighter on the size of libcore and simpler logic wise in core.

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

Matching `TryFrom` (a newer trait!) is a good solution.

Hey! It looks like you've submitted a new PR for the library teams!

If this PR contains changes to any `rust-lang/rust` public library APIs then please comment with `@rustbot label +T-libs-api -T-libs` to tag it appropriately. If this PR contains changes to any unstable APIs please edit the PR description to add a link to the relevant [API Change Proposal](https://std-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/feature-lifecycle/api-change-proposals.html) or [create one](https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/new?assignees=&labels=api-change-proposal%2C+T-libs-api&template=api-change-proposal.md&title=%28My+API+Change+Proposal%29) if you haven't already. If you're unsure where your change falls no worries, just leave it as is and the reviewer will take a look and make a decision to forward on if necessary.

Examples of `T-libs-api` changes:

* Stabilizing library features
* Introducing insta-stable changes such as new implementations of existing stable traits on existing stable types
* Introducing new or changing existing unstable library APIs (excluding permanently unstable features / features without a tracking issue)
* Changing public documentation in ways that create new stability guarantees
* Changing observable runtime behavior of library APIs

body:
I don't think the color changes are an improvement:

* Prelude items are not keywords. You can shadow them, they're part of the regular grammar, and many of them are plain library code with no special lang-item powers. Implying that `None` and `fn` are in some way the same thing seems like it would confuse beginners.

* Is making all keywords the same color actually a positive? It seems like the old color scheme intentionally made `&`, `*`, and `mut` their own color, separate from all other "keywords", because they're so heavily used. Making them the same color means, in function signatures, half the code is getting highlighted with the same shade of purple, which mostly defeats the purpose of syntax highlighting.

  ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1593513/193886936-2c8ba836-1e09-48b0-97c3-a3ebe625a7cb.png)

* If I was going to tweak the way literal expressions are highlighted, I'd make bool literals and numeric literals the same color, while giving *string* literals a separate color. Strings are special, because they can be arbitrarily long and contain text that looks like syntax (`"false"` and `false` are both valid), so it makes sense to want to distinguish them.

body:
> I guess we need an IndexMap because we iterate over this for interning?

Yes, from what I understand it is to make compilations reproducible as @/Aaron1011 explained:

> The iteration order of a HashMap depends on the Hash value of the keys. In rustc, the Hash value of a key can change between compilation sessions, even if the HashStable value remains the same (e.g. DefId, Symbol, etc.). This means that iterating over a HashMap can cause a query to produce different results given the same (as determined by HashStable) input. This can be quite subtle, as demonstrated by https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/82272#issuecomment-825124318

If we are sure that iterating over the `FxHashMap` in this case won't cause reproducibility issues, we could add comments explaining why that's the case.  The problem is, I don't think that is the case here (?). I'm not sure, as I'm new to this.

I also don't know if that regression is acceptable or not. 0.5% seems to be significant.
author: CastilloDel

body:
> If we are sure that iterating over the `FxHashMap` in this case won't cause reproducibility issues, we could add comments explaining why that's the case.

It doesn't cause problems here, because all we do is insert `Allocations` for already existing `AllocId`s into the TyCtxt. There is nothing that can possibly go wrong here from an ordering perspective. No matter the order, the end result is exactly the same.

body:
The general issue is https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/64552 - this fixes a particular instance by eliminating the need for rustc to attempt to prove a lifetime bound on the erased witness types.

As long as the new impl is sound, I think it's fine to merge this. However, users will continue to see these unhelpful errors in other cases until the underlying issue is resolved.

body:
How did you managed to get LLVM work on PSX? It's not officially supported target, though

I mean like, you cannot even cross compile to it from any other OS due to unsupported CPU architecture.
author: heavyrain266

body: LLVM supports MIPS-I at least partially. A quick search leads to at least one change for supporting it: https://reviews.llvm.org/D122427
author: bjorn3

body:
Yeah `-mcpu=mips1` was enabled in the patch @bjorn3 linked. That fixed the biggest issue which was miscompilations due to lack of support for load delay slots. The remaining issues are
- missing load delay slots in asm with `.set reorder`
- missing [coprocessor instructions](https://github.com/ayrtonm/psx-sdk-rs/issues/7)
- llvm tries lowering [`ATOMIC_FENCE`s](https://llvm.org/docs/Atomics.html) to a mips2 `sync` and crashes

The last one is the reason why atomics are currently disabled for this target and also means [`compiler_fence`s don't work](https://github.com/ayrtonm/psx-sdk-rs/issues/6#issue-1104580279), but there's a patch I'm planning on upstreaming.

author: lcnr

body:
@lcnr, yeah, sorry, I forgot to comment on this. 

There *is* a bigger underlying issue here, specifically using a raw type query on a type that hasn't been fully resolved. Ideally we'd be canonicalizing the types that we pass into this query and dealing with them more responsibly within a new infer ctxt, like we do when we check if a type is copy or sized. 

Luckily, the only type of inference variables that can leak into the queries at that point are region variables, which are erased, and int/float inference variables, which are fixed by this ICE. Unresolved type variables don't make it this far into generators I think.

I'll leave a note near the `ty.needs_drop` call in any case.
author: compiler-errors

body:
> using a raw type query on a type that hasn't been fully resolved.

I wonder if we should just plainly disallow stable-hashing of inference variables.  This would get rid of this hazard by a preemptive panic.

body:
> Luckily, the only type of inference variables that can leak into the queries at that point are region variables, which are erased, and int/float inference variables, which are fixed by this ICE. Unresolved type variables don't make it this far into generators I think.

surprising that int/float infer still exists here then, I feel like these also shouldn't appear during borrowck. Will look at this once I am back home next week.

Leaving a note there seems good enough for me 👍

this isn't during borrowck, this is in generator interior analysis during typeck, so I don't think we've done fallback on the integer variables at this point.

body:
when freshening each obligation by itself we have to correctly deal with inference constraints from the cyclic call. Otherwise we get the following issue:
```rust
trait Foo {} // assume `Foo` is coinductive here
struct Wrapper<T>(T);

impl<T> Foo for Wrapper<Wrapper<T>>
where
    Wrapper<T>: Foo
{} 
```
query: does `Wrapper<?0>: Foo` hold?
- candidate: `impl<T> Foo for Wrapper<Wrapper<T>>` -> `?0 -> Wrapper<?1>`
    - nested: `Wrapper<?1>: Foo` COINDUCTIVE CYCLE OK
- query returns `OK`: `?0 = Wrapper<?1>`

To deal with this evaluate has to return inference results which will only be added in the implementation of the trait system refactor initiative.

author: est31

body: Unfortunately it does not: the ICE in #100612 is caused by the panic [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/75ada3a1534fbc4801c73fafecd0f7455f1e3419/compiler/rustc_codegen_llvm/src/debuginfo/metadata/enums/native.rs#L420) in the code handling enums that have variants with fields, whereas this PR is for the code handling enums without any fields (C-style enums). While it is currently possible to pass the full 128 bits to LLVM for enums with fields too, LLVM currently truncates the discriminants of variants in debuginfo to 64 bits [here](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/617ca92bf155da73a8552345598a920777643e53/llvm/lib/CodeGen/AsmPrinter/DwarfUnit.cpp#L934-L937), whereas C-style enumerators are not truncated by LLVM when emitting DWARF.
author: beetrees

body: I see. It would be helpful though to have *some* kind of test.
author: est31

body: I agree, however I'm not sure what the best way to test it is. While this PR means that the DWARF is correctly emitted, neither of the two DWARF debuggers that are currently tested support 128-bit enums, with GDB stating `error reading variable: That operation is not available on integers of more than 8 bytes.` (this error also appears when trying to debug the stable `Option<NonZeroU128>`), and LLDB giving an assertion error `GetMaxU64 invalid byte_size!` (the same errors occur when trying to debug enums in C++ using `__uint128_t` as the discriminant type). The best idea I currently have is to add a test that uses the `llvm-dwarfdump` command to check that the enumerators are emitted correctly in the DWARF.
author: beetrees

body: Makes sense. I guess one can do as you suggest. IDK a test is not *that* important, but having one would still be preferable so that nothing regresses.

body: This is *nice*. My only thought here is that, because it's a very manual annotation, it will be forgotten. Is there any way we could maybe even get rid of the "end" annotation?
author: jackh726

body:
> because it's a very manual annotation, it will be forgotten

I agree, but seeing how this has tidied up some sorting errors already, it's hard to argue this isn't a step forward.

> Is there any way we could maybe even get rid of the "end" annotation?

Don't know if we want to get this advanced, but there are places in ui tests where we use regular expressions. The begin comment could contain a regular expression, then sort all nonempty lines that match that, perhaps sorting by a capture group. The downside would be that any change which causes one line to not match (like a comment in the middle of an argument list) would cause the elements below to not be sorted. So maybe we want a way to diagnose that... But now we're talking about tooling for the tools. Maybe a simple end delimiter is better.

I think we could get rid of the end annotation with more heuristics, but I think it's quite complex already and I don't think the end annotation is particularly annoying, so I'd rather not do this.

author: nbdd0121

body:
i686-mingw requires unwind tables to be registered with the unwinder when the module is loaded. We do this, but the problem in this case is that the cdylib has its own copy of libgcc statically linked into it. This is somewhat by design so that mingw executables don't have a runtime dependency on libgcc_s.dll, but it breaks cross-DLL unwinding since the respective unwinders are not aware of the unwind tables in other modules.

I think ignoring the test is fine in this case, but only on i686. Other architectures do not have this limitation.
author: Amanieu

> I think ignoring the test is fine in this case, but only on i686. Other architectures do not have this limitation.

Yeah, I tested this on x86_64 MinGW and it works fine. However we only have `ignore-x86` and `ignore-windows-gnu`, but not `ignore-(x86 and windows-gnu)`. Which directive should I use?

I think the actual problem here is that this implementation fails the goal of reducing code size impact in the caller: You are passing in a `fmt::Arguments`, which is a complex structure that requires a stack allocation. What you should be doing is only pass in a `&str` and then translate that to the formatting machinery internally.

This is probably also how it ends up failing the stack protector test.

WG-async is in favor of this change. Given that this feature is not widely used yet, if we take the fix it's better to do it sooner than later. However, changing the behavior of stable APIs that are safe but difficult to use correctly is without a lot of precedent, so we definitely want @rust-lang/libs-api's input. Given that we'd like to fix it sooner if we fix it, it might be worth considering pushing straight to beta or possibly even a 1.64.1 release. We'd want the @rust-lang/release's input on that though.

[Discussion on Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/187312-wg-async/topic/triage.20meeting.202022-10-10/near/303282893)
author: eholk

body:
Yes if we land this it should definitely be beta-backported. I don't know what our threshold is for a point release.

> It's probably unsound as-is -- or at least it makes the unsafe inside common patterns like pin_mut! unsound (when used inside the poll_fn).

As far as we know, it is not unsound. And it's not possible to use `pin_mut!` inside the `poll_fn` closure since that involves moving out of a local, so that macro simply cannot be used in an `FnMut` closure.

But if one uses `Pin::new_unchecked` directly, and forgets that this is pinning in a closure that is wrapped in a type that does pin its contents, then that is unsound.

body:
> Is there a clear example of a misuse that this PR fixes?

author: RalfJung

body:
> Nobody has spoken up in favor of that instance or given any motivation for it to exist.

Fact of the matter is that `poll_fn` is mostly used for writing trivial one-off futures, which are immediately `await`-ed, or passed to `block_on`, or to `task::spawn`. This means that the presence of `Unpin` impl doesn't matter that much in practice. This also means that your proposed change would have negligible benefit in practice.

But more generally, `PollFn: Unpin` obviously allows it to be passed into functions which require `Unpin` parameters. There are cases like that in the wild, even if rare. For example, take a look at [hyper](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/blob/0766d3f78d116ea243222cea134cfe7f418e6a3c/src/proto/h2/client.rs#L134). You can see that the `conn` future is constructed from a `poll_fn`, which is subsequently mapped, and passed into `conn_task`, which takes `conn: impl Future + Unpin`. It takes an `Unpin` future because it passes it to `futures_util::future::select`, which requires its parameters to be `Unpin`. `select` cannot pin its arguments inside the body, because it needs to return the remaining pending future, and values pinned to the stack can no longer be returned.

Now, you could `pin!` the `conn` future before passing it into `conn_task`, and that would work, but it's obviously worse ergonomics, and the same workaround can be used to make the inner closure `Unpin` as well. It's also impossible to pin a future if you want to return it, either from a function or from a nested scope. Consider this code:
```rust
let fut = {
    let f1 = ready(0);
    let f2 = poll_fn(|_cx| Poll::Ready(1));
    future::select(f1, f2)
};
// use `fut`
```

This looks like a reasonable code. It's easy to imagine a more complex variant, where `f1` would be some cancellation handle, while `f2` would be the computation you want to run. It's also impossible to write if `PollFn: !Unpin`. Not unless you pin the future to the heap, that is, but mandatory heap allocations is something we strongly strive to avoid in Rust.

Even more generally, `T: Unpin` is the always safe default, and so much easier to work with. It's safer, more ergonomic, less error-prone: 

* You don't need to use dangerous `Pin::new_unchecked` if you want to pin a `&mut T`.
* You don't need to take extra care in `Drop` impls to avoid accidentally moving some field, which may be hard to do in generic code.
* You  don't need to bother with pin projection, with the hard questions "what is safe to project", "how do I remember not to move projected data in `Drop`", "do I want good IDE experience and less macros, or a safer and more ergonomic way to pin-project".
* You don't need to pin your futures before you poll them, which is an ergonomic loss at best, and a heap allocation at worst (as discussed above).
* You can use a type as generic parameter, without carrying all the pin projection troubles to the generic type, which likely doesn't care about pinning in the first place.
* You can put `impl Future + Unpin` in a collection and directly poll it. With `!Unpin`, you must pin them beforehand (which again will require allocations).

So the default should be "everything is  `Unpin` unless there's a good reason not to be" (i.e. you're writing a self-referential type, or want to pin-project), and `poll_fn` (and more generally other combinators taking closures) don't have that good reason.

body:
> This looks like a reasonable code.

Captureless closures are `Unpin` so nothing changes for them with this PR.

The proposal is for `PollFn` to propagate `Unpin` like it propagates `Send` and `Sync`, and like most types propagate (or should propagate) `Unpin`.

> So the default should be "everything is Unpin unless there's a good reason not to be" (i.e. you're writing a self-referential type, or want to pin-project), and poll_fn (and more generally other combinators taking closures) don't have that good reason.

This makes sense for self-contained types, but not for type combinators. Type combinators must respect the good reasons their users might have to be `!Unpin`. The problem with the current approach is that *even if the user has a good reason for things not to be `Unpin`, `PollFn` forces them to be `Unpin`*. That's bad.
author: RalfJung

body:
> Even more generally, T: Unpin is the always safe default

That's only true if you're *consuming* a future - you can throw `T: Unpin` bounds on your apis, write only safe code, and let your callers worry about pinning (by taking advantage of that fact that `Box<SomeType>` is always `Unpin`,  for example).

However, if you're *writing* a future (and more specifically, writing an `Unpin` impl), you need to be very careful. The  `pin-project` crate generates an `Unpin` impl that makes sure to respect your declared pin-projections. Hoever, the current `poll_fn` API commits you to *not* performing pin-projections, without any kind of explicit acknowledgment of this fact in your code. This may be "safe" in the technical sense of not requiring `unsafe`, but I think it's a large potential fotogun.

What you are saying is, to me, equivalent to saying "we could add `impl<T: Send> Sync for Vec<T>`", since after all the combinator can add locks for synchronization, for all the users care. It's technically correct but also nothing I think anyone would ever expect `Vec` to do.

With combinators, the inner types are usually *literally the only thing defining the properties of the whole*. That's what makes them generic compositonal combinators. So I really have no idea how it could be reasonable for `PollFn` to act differently here.

> Unpin is basically lint-level. It's just a performance and ergonomic optimization. 

No, that's very  far from the truth. `Unpin` is a fundamental statement about the invariants of this type, specifically stating that any pinned value of this type can be transmuted into an unpinned value of this type. This is very similar to `Send` and `Sync`. It just happens to be the case that a bad `Unpin` *on its own* (without other `unsafe` code) cannot cause UB, and hence the `Unpin` trait was made safe. That probably was a mistake.

(FWIW, a bad `Send`/`Sync` on its own also cannot cause UB, you need something like `thread::spawn` to cause UB. But that is in the standard library so the traits were made unsafe. Pin projections were not in the standard library so `Unpin` was made safe.)

body:
> The discussion is specifically about the end users of poll_fn, not about its (simple) implementation, so I don't see how your comment is relevant.

Users of `poll_fn` *are* writing futures - they're just relying on `poll_fn` to make the implementation simpler. Having `PollFn` implement `Unpin` unconditionally is equivalent to hand-writing a struct implementing `Future`, and then adding a explicit unconditional `Unpin` impl. It's explicitly overriding the default behavior (the structural auto-trait impl of `Unpin`), and requires additional thought. 

Unlike a hand-written struct, `poll_fn` is making this non-default choice without knowing anything about the implementation of the future. While we *could* decide that this is the correct choice, and document this behavior (shifting the "blame"  to the unsafe code constructing the `Pin`), I think it's the wrong choice. `Unpin` is a very subtle trait to work with, and I don't think we should be making it even harder by adding foot guns in the standard library.

Because `FnMut::call_mut` takes a `&mut Self`, not a `Pin<&mut Self>`.

Inside the closure, you can just move/swap/exchange/assign the moved `future`, regardless of the proposed change. (Macros like `pin_mut!()` and `pin!()` will prevent that from happening.)

> What you are saying is, to me, equivalent to saying "we could add impl<T: Send> Sync for Vec<T>", since after all the combinator can add locks for synchronization, for all the users care.

As far as the creator of `T` knows or cares, yes, this is what may happen. You cannot rely that if your `T: !Sync` is a generic parameter in `Foo<_>`, then `Foo<T>: !Sync`. The author of `Foo<_>` may decide otherwise. Not that I can imagine how it would be even possible to rely on that.

>
> No, that's very far from the truth.

For self-referential types, yes. For combinators, no. It is closer in guarantees to `UnwindSafe` than to `Send/Sync`, since it doesn't significantly change the possible programs. It's basically a matter of where you pin. 

If a field of a struct is `!Send/!Sync`, then the structure itself may never be soundly `Send/Sync`. For `Unpin`, that's not the case.

-------

Actually, forget all that. I stand by the general principles I talk about, but they are irrelevant to the specific discussion. Making `PollFn<F>: !Unpin` wouldn't change anything with regards to safety, because you need `&mut F` to call `FnMut::call_mut`. If you project `PollFn<F> -> F` structurally, you can't call the closure, and would need to turn `Pin<&mut F> -> &mut F`, which is explicitly unsound, since you can't assume anything about `F`. If you project non-structurally, you're in the same situation as now, except using `PollFn<F>` becomes less convenient.

If you take a look at the standard combinators on `Stream` and `Future`, none of them pins the inner closure, precisely because a pinned closure is either unusable or unsound. And if none of your fields are pinned, what's the point of pinning the struct?

author: RalfJung

body:
> It is closer in guarantees to UnwindSafe than to Send/Sync, since it doesn't significantly change the possible programs. It's basically a matter of where you pin.

No that's just not true. It seems like the fact that `Unpin` was made safe lead to some heavy misunderstandings about what `Unpin` does or means. :(

`Unpin` makes a very specific statement about how the invariants of the "pinned" and "unpinned" typestates relate -- I elaborated on this [years ago in this blog post](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2018/04/05/a-formal-look-at-pinning.html). By writing `impl Unpin` you are implicitly also making statements about your type's invariants.

> If a field of a struct is !Send/!Sync, then the structure itself may never be soundly Send/Sync.

Of course it may be. If the field is private and never used, for example, then making it Send/Sync is entirely sound. Another option is to add run-time checks or synchronization -- `Mutex` adds `Sync` even if the field is not `Sync`; that is in fact its entire point. This is a deep statement about what `Mutex` does with the invariants of its inner type. The same is true for `Unpin`, except that we don't need any run-time checks to ensure that adding `Unpin` is sound, we just need to declare that our pinned typestate is like our unpinned typestate, and make sure nobody writes any unsafe code that assumes the opposite. But this is subtle, because the usual expectation is that the pinned typestate of a struct is just the pinned typestate of all its fields (that's how our type invariants are propagated everywhere else) -- an `impl Unpin` says that we deviate from this default and do something special.

The fact that `Unpin` is a safe trait while `Send`/`Sync` are not is an accident caused by the fact that `Pin` was "bolted on" way after Rust 1.0 and that we don't have native support for pin projections. It does *not* indicate any fundamental difference between the nature of these traits. (`UnwindSafe`, on the other hand, is completely different and never had a proper safety contract associated with it.)

> If you take a look at the standard combinators on Stream and Future, none of them pins the inner closure, precisely because a pinned closure is either unusable or unsound.

This is just factually wrong, and I don't understand why you keep repeating statements like this. The pinned closure capture in `futures`/`tokio` would be entirely sound if they used the version of `poll_fn` from this PR.

body:
From what I could gather from this thread, the opposing arguments boil down to "The API is sound as it currently is", and "This doesn't matter in practice". I believe that going for the C++ philosophy of blaming the user instead of fixing an error prone API is unfavorable to the project. 

And this idea that it "does not matter in practice" is unfathomable to me. Most future types that will ever exist in the ecosystem are `!Unpin`. Therefore, not supporting `Pin` projection implies that `poll_fn` can never be used to compose the majority of futures. Naturally, there is a myriad of reasons for which you may want to compose `!Unpin` futures with `poll_fn`, so I see this as a pointless restriction. 
 
I think this PR has met its burden of proof. The crater run shows that there is no ecosystem breakage, and two of the most widely used async crates have fallen for this footgun. Additionally, it strictly increases the usefulness of this API. 

Conversely, I don't think the opposition has met theirs. We are yet to see a use case for the current behavior. That is, capturing `!Unpin` values, yet expecting `PollFn: Unpin`. And I'd argue that even in those cases, the fix is just a matter of calling `Pin::new_unchecked` instead of `Pin::new`. I feel that half of the opposing arguments are lengthy explanations of why `PollFn` is sound as it is (which was never questioned). While the other half are use cases that are not affected by this PR.
